title: Bear wrongs patiently
hookLine: bear with an injury without revenge
tomorrow: pray for the dead, or ask the dead to pray for us?

lines: TURN TO HIM ALSO THE OTHER.
cards: The ref misses the elbow, the player who threw it smirks, and the urge is to even the score. Jesus seems to have settled it. In the Douay-Rheims: "if one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other."
But here's the odd part. At his trial, a servant of the high priest strikes Jesus. And Jesus doesn't turn the other cheek.
He answers back: "If I have spoken evil, give testimony of the evil; but if well, why strikest thou me?"

teach.h: HE NAMES IT; HE DOESN'T STRIKE.
teach.b: So which is it? The puzzle solves itself once you see what Jesus doesn't do. He doesn't strike back.

He doesn't curse the man or plan to get even later. He names the wrong, calmly, and asks for the truth. Peter's first letter remembers him this way: insulted, he didn't insult back; suffering, he made no threats.
So bearing wrongs patiently, on the traditional list of spiritual works of mercy, isn't pretending a wrong is fine. It's refusing to answer it with revenge.
Paul gives the rule to the Romans: "To no man rendering evil for evil."
And a few lines later: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good."

Here's one for the drive home: some readers point out that a blow to the right cheek from a right hand would be a backhand, more insult than attack, so the saying may be about insults. That's one reading, not a ruling.
And one thing it never means: staying where you aren't safe. The Catechism still allows legitimate defense, and protecting others can be a duty. This work is about my own grudge.
In practice it looks like the snide comment you don't answer in kind, the slight at work you let go, the foul you report to the ref instead of repaying.
Bear it, and if the truth needs saying, say it calmly.

how: Catholics count bearing wrongs patiently among the spiritual works of mercy and often join small, unavenged injuries to prayer, while the Church teaches that legitimate defense and seeking justice remain allowed.

o: wait quietly for a wrong to be fixed
take an injury without paying it back
put up with pain and never complain

games.q: the cheek and the trial — tap the pairs.
p: turn to him also the other
to no man rendering evil for evil

s: turn the other cheek means never speaking up when wronged
struck at his trial, Jesus asked why strikest thou me? he named the wrong without striking back.
Paul tells the Romans to overcome evil by good
be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good (Romans 12:21).
bearing wrongs patiently means staying where you aren't safe
it's about refusing revenge. the Catechism still allows legitimate defense.

games.q: a coworker keeps taking credit for your ideas in meetings. next week you could do the same to him. what fits Romans 12?
o: don't repay it; calmly say whose idea it was, and keep working well.
repay it once so he learns how it feels, and then call it even.
say nothing, ever; bearing wrongs means letting him keep at it.
games.why: Paul says render no one evil for evil, and overcome evil by good. Jesus at his trial named the wrong without striking back.

practice: Close your eyes and replay one small slight from this week: a comment, a look, a door shut in your face.
Feel the comeback rise, and instead of rehearsing it, breathe out slowly and let it go unanswered, like a ball you choose not to chase. If you pray, you can pray for the person who did it.

wordCard.voice: Bear wrongs patiently. Take an injury without paying it back, and name it honestly if it needs naming.

orig.note: Latin: patiently. from the traditional Latin list of the works of mercy.

carryVoice: Your line: bear it. No revenge, though the truth can still be spoken calmly. Sleep well.
